A '''dual-clutch transmission''' ('''DCT''') (sometimes referred to as a '''twin-clutch transmission''') is a type of multi-speed [[motor vehicle|vehicle]] [[Transmission (mechanics)|transmission system]], that uses two separate [[clutch]]es for odd and even [[gear train|gear sets]].<ref name=AMS>{{cite journal|title=Powertrain — transmissions: Shift in power to the gearbox|url=http://www.unofficialbmw.com/images/SHIFT1.pdf|journal=[[Auto, Motor und Sport|AMS]]|publisher=UnofficialBMW.com|date=September–October 2003|access-date=31 October 2009|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717164509/http://www.unofficialbmw.com/images/SHIFT1.pdf|archive-date=17 July 2011}}</ref> The design is often similar to two separate [[manual transmission]]s with their respective clutches contained within one housing, and working as one unit.<ref name=AEI>{{cite journal|title=Automatic-shifting dual-clutch transmissions are poised to grab share from traditional transmissions thanks to their combination of efficiency and convenience|url=http://www.dctfacts.com/documents/1-117-6-20.pdf|journal=AEI-online.org|publisher=DCTfacts.com|date=June 2009|access-date=31 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007173150/http://www.dctfacts.com/documents/1-117-6-20.pdf|archive-date=7 October 2011}}</ref><ref name=PorschePDK_Glossary>{{cite web |title=Porsche Doppelkupplung (PDK) |url=http://www.porsche.com/microsite/technology/default.aspx?pool=uk&ShowSingleTechterm=PTPDopKuGe&Category=&Model=&SearchedString=&SelectedVariant= |publisher=Porsche.com |access-date=31 October 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205135604/http://www.porsche.com/microsite/technology/default.aspx?pool=uk&ShowSingleTechterm=PTPDopKuGe&Category=&Model=&SearchedString=&SelectedVariant= |archive-date=5 December 2008 }}</ref> In car and truck applications, the DCT functions as an [[automatic transmission]], requiring no driver input to change gears.

The first DCT to reach production was the ''Easidrive'' automatic transmission introduced on the [[Hillman_Minx#Audax_design_Hillman_Minx_(Series_I_to_Series_VI,_1956–1967)|1961 Hillman Minx]] mid-size car. This was followed by various eastern European tractors through the 1970s (using manual operation via a single clutch pedal), then the [[Porsche 962|Porsche 962 C]] racing car in 1985. The first DCT of the modern era was used in the 2003 [[Volkswagen Golf Mk4#R32 (2003)|Volkswagen Golf R32]]. Since the late 2000s, DCTs have become increasingly widespread, and have supplanted hydraulic automatic transmissions in various models of cars.

More generally, a transmission with several clutches can be called a '''multi clutch transmission'''. For example, the [[Koenigsegg Jesko]] has a transmission with one clutch per gear,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.roadandtrack.com/new-cars/car-technology/a28230198/koenigsegg-jesko-seven-clutch-gearbox-how-it-works/|title=Here's How the Koenigsegg Jesko's Seven-Clutch Gearbox Works|first=Jason|last=Fenske|date=July 8, 2019|website=Road & Track}}</ref> making for a total of 7 clutches.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.motortrend.com/reviews/koenigsegg-light-speed-transmission-manual-automatic-how-it-works-explained/|title=Holy Shift! Koenigsegg's Wild Manual Transmission Has 7 Clutches—and an Automatic Mode|date=August 19, 2022|website=MotorTrend}}</ref><ref name="Car and Driver">{{cite web|url=https://www.caranddriver.com/features/a28927301/koenigsegg-new-transmission-promises-ultraquick-shifts/|title=Koenigsegg's New Light Speed Transmission Promises Ultraquick Shifts|date=14 September 2019|first=K.C.|last=Colwell|publisher=[[Car and Driver]]|access-date=14 September 2019|archive-date=17 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190917225917/https://www.caranddriver.com/features/a28927301/koenigsegg-new-transmission-promises-ultraquick-shifts/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Design ==
[[File:VW DSG transmission DTMB.jpg|thumb|DCT based on a concentric clutch layout (inside the round black cover, shown in the center of the image)]]

The fundamental principle of a DCT is that one clutch drives a gear-set for the even-numbered gears, while the other clutch drives the odd-numbered gears.<ref name=AMS/><ref name=AEI/><ref name=VMS/> Since the DCT can pre-select an odd gear while the vehicle is being propelled in an even gear (or vice versa), DCTs can shift several times faster than is possible with a manual transmission.<ref name=PorschePDK_Glossary/><ref name=Eureka/> By timing the operation of one clutch to engage at the precise moment that the other is disengaging, a DCT can shift gears without interrupting the torque supply to the wheels.<ref name=VMS/><ref name=Eureka/>

A DCT uses clutch packs (as per a manual transmission), rather than the [[torque converter]] used by traditional (hydraulic) automatic transmissions.<ref name=AMS/> The DCT clutches are either "wet" or "dry" and are similar to the clutches used in most motorcycles.<ref name=DCTfactsWet>{{cite web|url=http://www.dctfacts.com/information/wet-clutch-or-dry-clutch.aspx|title=Wet-Clutch or Dry-Clutch?|publisher=The Lubrizol Corporation|work=DCTfacts.com|access-date=30 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100327162942/http://www.dctfacts.com/information/wet-clutch-or-dry-clutch.aspx|archive-date=27 March 2010}}</ref> Wet-clutches are bathed in oil to provide cooling for the clutch surface,<ref name=VWAG7/> therefore wet-clutches are often used in applications with higher torque loads, such as the {{convert|1250|Nm|0|abbr=on}} engine in the [[Bugatti Veyron]].

Several arrangements for the two clutches are possible, and are outlined below:
* Most automotive DCTs use two [[concentric]] clutch packs located on the same axis as the [[flywheel]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Two Clutches, No Waiting |url=https://www.corvette-mag.com/issues/135/articles/two-clutches-no-waiting |website=www.corvette-mag.com |access-date=23 July 2020 |language=en-us}}</ref> Therefore, the outer clutch pack has a larger diameter than the inner clutch pack.
* Many DCTs for tractors (such as the [[Fortschritt ZT 320]]) use a similar arrangement where the clutches are located on the same axis of the flywheel. The difference is that the clutches are at different positions on this axis (i.e. one in front of the other) and the same size as each other.<ref>{{cite web |title=ZT300 doppelkupplung image |url=https://www.ddr-landmaschinen.de/webbilder/sonderseite/zt300_doppelkupplung.jpg |website=www.ddr-landmaschinen.de |access-date=25 July 2020}}</ref> This design is used by the ''Tremec TR-9070'' DCT used by the 2020 [[Shelby Mustang#Ford Performance 3rd generation Shelby GT500 (2020–2022)|Ford Mustang Shelby GT500]].<ref>{{cite web |title=TREMEC Introduces New 7-Speed Dual Clutch Transmission |url=https://eastsidemotorsports.com/blogs/news/tremec-introduces-new-7-speed-dual-clutch-transmission |website=www.eastsidemotorsports.com |access-date=25 July 2020}}</ref>
* Another design (as used by the ''Volkswagen DQ200'' transmission)<ref name=AEI/><ref name=VWAG7/> arranges two identical-size clutches located side-by-side. This design requires two side-by-side input shafts, which are driven from the crankshaft via gears.

== History ==
[[Image:Cambio a doppia frizione.svg|thumb|right|Schematic diagram of a type of dual-clutch gearbox:{{unbulleted list
| M: Motor
| A: Primary drive and driving shaft
| B: Dual clutch
| C: Driven shaft
| D: Layshaft, hollow, even gears
| E: Layshaft, odd gears
| F: Output
}}]]

The concept of a dual-clutch transmission was invented by French engineer [[Adolphe Kégresse]] in 1939.<ref>{{cite web |title=How dual-clutch transmission works |url=https://www.hyundai.news/eu/stories/how-dual-clutch-transmission-works/ |website=www.hyundai.com |access-date=20 July 2020 |language=en}}</ref> The transmission was intended for use in the [[Citroën Traction Avant]], however Kégresse ran out of money before a working model could be developed.<ref>{{cite web |title=How Dual-clutch Transmissions Work |url=https://auto.howstuffworks.com/dual-clutch-transmission3.htm |website=www.howstuffworks.com |access-date=20 July 2020 |language=en |date=6 April 2006}}</ref>

One of the first production DCTs was the ''Easidrive'' unit developed in the late 1950s by [[United Kingdom]]'s [[Smiths Industries]] and [[Rootes Group|Rootes]]. This DCT – introduced on the 1961 [[Hillman Minx#Audax design Hillman Minx (Series I to Series VI, 1956–67)|Hillman Minx (Series IIIC)]] – used two [[Electromagnetic clutch|electro-magnetic clutches]], along with analogue [[electronics]] and a series of [[solenoid]]s to implement the gear shifts.<ref>{{cite web |title=Easidrive |url=http://www.andymurkin.net/Hillman/Hillinfo/Easidrive.html |website=www.andymurkin.net |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=A Useful Text-Book - The Motor Vehicle |url=https://www.motorsportmagazine.com/archive/article/august-1962/31/a-useful-text-book |website=www.motorsportmagazine.com |date=7 July 2014 |access-date=20 July 2020}}</ref> The ''Easidrive'' was offered as an option on Hillman and Singer models, however it was not a reliable device and many were replaced by conventional manual transmissions.

[[Porsche]] began development of DCTs for racing cars in the late 1970s,<ref>{{cite web |title=The PDK Transmission |url=https://www.excellence-mag.com/issues/226/articles/the-pdk-transmission?page=3 |website=www.excellence-mag.com |access-date=21 July 2020 |language=en-us}}</ref> due to the possibility of a DCT preventing a drop in boost during gear shifts on a turbocharged engine.<ref>{{cite web |title=Shift This: A History of Porsche's Sportomatic, Tiptronic, and PDK Transmissions |url=https://www.caranddriver.com/news/a15366473/shift-this-a-history-of-porsches-sportomatic-tiptronic-and-pdk-transmissions/ |website=www.caranddriver.com |access-date=21 July 2020 |date=10 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Porsche 956 |url=https://www.stuttcars.com/porsche-models/956/ |website=www.stuttcars.com |date=10 May 2010 |access-date=21 July 2020 |language=en}}</ref> As the electronics required to control the transmission became compact enough to be practical, the ''Porsche Doppelkupplungsgetriebe'' ('dual-clutch gearbox') (PDK) transmission was installed as a prototype in a [[Porsche 956]] Le Mans racing car in 1983.<ref name=AEI/><ref>{{cite web |title=Here's What the Porsche PDK Gearbox Means |url=https://www.thedrive.com/porsche/17878/watch-this-brief-history-of-porsches-pdk-gearbox |website=www.thedrive.com |date=22 January 2018 |access-date=21 July 2020}}</ref> The first use of a PDK in competition was the 1985 [[Porsche 962|Porsche 962 C]] Le Mans racing car, which won the [[World Sportscar Championship]] in 1986.<ref name=AEI/><ref>{{cite web |title=Porsche 962 and PDK transmission |url=https://flatsixes.com/cars/porsche-962/introducing-porsche-factoids/ |website=www.flatsixes.com |access-date=21 July 2020 |date=24 October 2008}}</ref> The PDK transmission was also used in the 1985 [[Audi Quattro S1|Audi Sport Quattro S1]] Group B rally car.<ref name=Eureka>{{cite web|title=Dual clutches take the lead|url=http://www.eurekamagazine.co.uk/article/17517/Dual-clutches-take-the-lead.aspx|publisher=Findlay Media Ltd|work=Eureka Magazine|date=13 March 2009|access-date=31 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091020184735/http://www.eurekamagazine.co.uk/article/17517/Dual-clutches-take-the-lead.aspx|archive-date=20 October 2009}}</ref><ref name=Lufteknic>{{cite web|title=The Porsche Transmission|url=http://www.lufteknic.com/trans.html#Tiptronic|work=Lüfteknic.com|access-date=28 October 2009|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091106102002/http://www.lufteknic.com/trans.html#Tiptronic|archive-date=6 November 2009}}</ref>

The first mass-production passenger car to use a DCT was the 2003 [[Volkswagen Golf Mk4#R32|Volkswagen Golf R32]].<ref name=AEI/><ref name=VMS>{{cite press release|title=Volkswagen DSG — World's first dual-clutch gearbox in a production car|publisher=[[Volkswagen AG]]|work=Volkswagen-Media-Services.com|date=22 November 2002|url=https://www.volkswagen-media-services.com/medias_publish/ms/content/en/pressemitteilungen/2002/11/22/volkswagen_dsg_-_world.standard.gid-oeffentlichkeit.html|access-date=30 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060524093743/http://www.volkswagen-media-services.com/medias_publish/ms/content/en/pressemitteilungen/2002/11/22/volkswagen_dsg_-_world.standard.gid-oeffentlichkeit.html|archive-date=24 May 2006}}</ref><ref name=VWAG7>{{cite web|title=The 7-speed DSG — the intelligent automatic gearbox from Volkswagen|publisher=[[Volkswagen AG]]|work=VolkswagenAG.com|date=21 January 2008|url=http://www.volkswagenag.com/vwag/vwcorp/info_center/en/themes/2008/01/the_7speed_dsg.html|access-date=30 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101216093140/http://www.volkswagenag.com/vwag/vwcorp/info_center/en/themes/2008/01/the_7speed_dsg.html|archive-date=16 December 2010}}</ref>

[[Honda]] manufactures DCTs for some Honda motorcycles as of 2024, and was the first to add a DCT to motorcycles. Honda also previously manufactured DCTs for some [[Acura]] cars.

[[List_of_Hyundai_transmissions#Dual_Clutch_Transmission_(DCT)|HYUNDAI TRANSYS]] manufactures dry 7-speed and wet 8-speed DCTs as of 2024. The DCTs are used in some Hyundai and Kia (e.g. Ceed) vehicles.

== Usage in motor vehicles ==
<!-- Note: Given the widespread usage of DCTs in recent times, this section should not be an indiscriminate list of cars that use a DCT. Please only include events that are historically significant.-->
Following its 2003 introduction in the [[Volkswagen Golf Mk4#R32|Volkswagen Golf R32]], a 6-speed DCT (model code ''DQ250''), with two wet-clutches arranged concentrically, has been used in several Volkswagen and Audi models.<ref name=VWAG7/> In 2008, Volkswagen group began production of the ''DQ200'', a 7-speed DCT using two dry-clutches arranged side-by-side (instead of concentrically).<ref name=VWAG7/><ref name=AEI/> Volkswagen claims fuel economy improvements of 6% compared with a 6-speed manual and 20% compared with a traditional (hydraulic) automatic transmission.<ref name=VWAG7/> DCT transmissions have been used on vehicles sold by Alfa Romeo, Volkswagen, Audi, Tata Motors, SEAT, Skoda, and Bugatti, mostly marketed using the term ''Direct-Shift Gearbox'' (except for Alfa Romeo, which has used the term TCT, also Tata Motors uses the term DCA (Dual Clutch Automatic) and Audi, which has also used the term ''S-Tronic'').<ref name=Eureka/><ref>{{citation|title=Volkswagen Service Training Manual 308 — 02E 6-speed DSG}}</ref><ref name="AutoChannel" />

Usage in high performance cars began in 2005 with the 7-speed DCT used in the [[Bugatti Veyron]]. Other early high performance applications include the 2007 [[Nissan GT-R]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sae.org/automag/technewsletter/080205Tech/04.htm|title=BorgWarner DCT for Nissan's GT-R|publisher=SAE International|work=SAE.org|access-date=28 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091119194907/http://www.sae.org/automag/technewsletter/080205Tech/04.htm|archive-date=19 November 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aichikikai.co.jp/english/history.html |title=Aichi Kikai manufacturing history |publisher=Aichi Machine Industry Co., Ltd |work=AichiKikai.co.jp |access-date=7 July 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100819051523/http://www.aichikikai.co.jp/english/history.html |archive-date=August 19, 2010 }}</ref> the 2008 [[Ferrari California]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dctfacts.com/lapp_pg3a.asp |title=Ferrari chooses DCT for its latest supercar |publisher=The Lubrizol Corporation |work=DCTfacts.com |access-date=30 October 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091010073320/http://www.dctfacts.com/lapp_pg3a.asp |archive-date=October 10, 2009 }}</ref> the 2008 [[Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution#Evolution X|Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution X]]<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://media.mitsubishi-motors.com/pressrelease/e/corporate/detail1657.html|title=Mitsubishi Motors develops S-AWC vehicle dynamics control system & Twin Clutch SST automated manual transmission|publisher=Mitsubishi Motors|date=10 July 2007|access-date=28 October 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929091739/http://media.mitsubishi-motors.com/pressrelease/e/corporate/detail1657.html|archive-date=29 September 2007|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref name=EdmundsEvoX>{{cite web |url=http://blogs.edmunds.com/roadtests/2009/05/2008-mitsubishi-lancer-evolution-x-mr-are-shift-paddles-for-wimps.html |title=2008 Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution X MR: Are Shift Paddles for Wimps? |publisher=Edmunds Inc. |work=Blogs.Edmunds.com |date=2009-05-06 |access-date=28 October 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090510225942/http://blogs.edmunds.com/roadtests/2009/05/2008-mitsubishi-lancer-evolution-x-mr-are-shift-paddles-for-wimps.html |archive-date=10 May 2009 }}</ref><ref name=TheMotorReport>{{cite web|url=http://www.themotorreport.com.au/4259/ss-t-the-magic-inside-the-evo-x/|title=SS-T: The Magic Inside the Evo X|publisher=The Motor Report Pty. Ltd.|work=TheMotorReport.com.au|date=14 April 2008|access-date=28 October 2009|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090829074838/http://www.themotorreport.com.au/4259/ss-t-the-magic-inside-the-evo-x/|archive-date=29 August 2009}}</ref> and the 2009 [[Porsche 997|Porsche 911 (997)]].<ref name=PorschePress>{{cite press release|title=New Porsche 911 with Direct Fuel Injection and Double-Clutch Gearbox|url=http://www.porsche.com/uk/aboutporsche/pressreleases/pag/archive2008/quarter2/?pool=international-de&id=2008-06-06-01|publisher=Porsche Cars Great Britain Ltd. / Dr. Ing. h.c. F. Porsche AG|date=6 June 2008|access-date=31 October 2009}}</ref><ref name=PorschePDK_Glossary911>{{cite web|title=Porsche Doppelkupplung (PDK) — 911 Carrera & 911 Targa 4 Models|url=http://www.porsche.com/microsite/technology/default.aspx?pool=uk&ShowSingleTechterm=PTPDopKuGe&Category=&Model=&SearchedString=&SelectedVariant=PMT911CarreraTarga|publisher=Dr. Ing. h.c. F. Porsche AG|work=Porsche.com|access-date=31 October 2009}}</ref>

The 2009 [[Honda VFR1200F]] is the first motorcycle to use a DCT.<ref>{{cite web | url= http://www.motorcycle-usa.com/625/4795/Motorcycle-Article/2010-Honda-VFR1200F-First-Look.aspx | work= Motorcycle USA | title= 2010 Honda VFR1200F First Look | date= 8 October 2009 | first= Steve | last= Atlas | access-date= 31 October 2009 | url-status= dead | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091011065818/http://www.motorcycle-usa.com/625/4795/Motorcycle-Article/2010-Honda-VFR1200F-First-Look.aspx | archive-date= 11 October 2009 | df= dmy-all }}</ref>  Honda has since expanded the application of the DCT to the Gold Wing model (model year 2018), the Africa Twin, the NT1100, Rebel 1100, and the NC700XD (model year 2012).

In 2010, the [[Fuso (company)|Mitsubishi Fuso]] 6-speed ''Duonic'' transmission became the first DCT to be used in a truck.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://media.daimler.com/dcmedia/0-921-854990-1-1316186-1-0-0-0-0-1-11701-614240-0-1-0-0-0-0-0.html|title=First double-clutch transmission in a truck |website=www.daimler.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111004064335/http://media.daimler.com/dcmedia/0-921-854990-1-1316186-1-0-0-0-0-1-11701-614240-0-1-0-0-0-0-0.html|archive-date=4 October 2011}}</ref>

The 2015 [[Acura TLX]] uses a [[torque converter]] (a device typically used in hydraulic automatic transmissions) paired with its 8-speed DCT. The purpose of the torque converter is to improve the smoothness of low-speed driving, through the elimination of jolting and shuddering sometimes found in DCTs at low speed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Honda's new 8-speed DCT uses a torque converter |url=https://www.sae.org/site/news/2014/08/hondas-new-8-speed-dct-uses-a-torque-converter |access-date=2024-08-04 |website=www.sae.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Usage in tractors  ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=May 2026}}
Several 1970s tractors from eastern European countries (such as the [[Kirovets K-700]] derivatives) used manually operated DCTs. For example, the [[Fortschritt ZT 300]] has an ''Unterlastschaltstufe'' ('shifting under load') function, which needs to be pre-selected by the driver and then activated by pressing the clutch halfway down. This engages the second clutch, which applies a reduction gear to the driven wheels without any interruption in the torque transmission to the wheels.

extract:
A dual-clutch transmission (DCT) (sometimes referred to as a twin-clutch transmission) is a type of multi-speed vehicle transmission system, that uses two separate clutches for odd and even gear sets. The design is often similar to two separate manual transmissions with their respective clutches contained within one housing, and working as one unit. In car and truck applications, the DCT functions as an automatic transmission, requiring no driver input to change gears.
The first DCT to reach production was the Easidrive automatic transmission introduced on the 1961 Hillman Minx mid-size car. This was followed by various eastern European tractors through the 1970s (using manual operation via a single clutch pedal), then the Porsche 962 C racing car in 1985. The first DCT of the modern era was used in the 2003 Volkswagen Golf R32. Since the late 2000s, DCTs have become increasingly widespread, and have supplanted hydraulic automatic transmissions in various models of cars.
More generally, a transmission with several clutches can be called a multi clutch transmission. For example, the Koenigsegg Jesko has a transmission with one clutch per gear, making for a total of 7 clutches.
